name: Pheromone cologne

card.summary: Scents sold with the claim that added pheromones make the wearer more attractive; reviewers say no human pheromone has been shown to change behavior.
card.aka: Pheromone perfume, pheromone body spray, smellmaxxing
card.note: Marketing claims of sexual attraction are described by reviewers as unsupported by peer-reviewed evidence.

quick.overview:
Pheromone colognes are fragrances or sprays sold with the claim that they contain human sex pheromones that increase attraction. The concept draws on research into compounds such as androstenone and androstadienone.

A widely cited encyclopedia summary says no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behavior, and describes the area as speculative and controversial.
quick.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms involve steroid compounds from sweat glands acting through the vomeronasal organ or olfactory receptors. The human vomeronasal organ is described as atrophied or absent in adults with nonfunctional receptor genes, and whether it detects pheromones is disputed.
quick.risks: Reported direct risks are those of any fragrance product, such as skin irritation or allergy in some users. The main caveat reviewers raise is that effects on attraction are not demonstrated.

lead: Pheromone cologne is a fragrance or body spray sold with the claim that it contains human pheromones that make the wearer more attractive. Buyers use it as a scent layer on top of grooming, hoping it boosts how appealing they come across, particularly to women; marketing phrases such as 'increase attractiveness' and 'irresistible scent' are common [1][2]. In looksmaxxing circles scent is treated as one more part of presentation, and Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing mentions offshoots such as smellmaxxing [3].

The compounds typically named in products are steroid-like molecules from sweat and other secretions: androstadienone, androstenone, androstenol and estratetraenol [2]. The word 'pheromone' was coined in 1959 [4]. A 1978 study (Kirk-Smith) had people wearing masks treated with androstenol rate photographed faces as warmer and more friendly, and later studies examined mood and attention effects of androstadienone [4]. Wikipedia reports that the field has been marked by small samples, publication bias and weak methods, and that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behaviour, a statement the page marks as disputed [4].

Grokipedia notes that benefits users perceive are widely attributed to placebo effects or to the pleasant qualities of the fragrance itself, and that pheromone colognes follow standard eau-de-cologne construction with alcohol, fixatives and musk, amber, woody or vanilla base notes [2].

chain: Fragrance containing added synthetic pheromone compounds is sprayed on
Wearer smells good and, per marketing, signals attraction
Aim: more positive reactions from others
angle.text: People wear pheromone colognes to add a pleasant scent and, as advertised, a chemical attraction signal. The cologne itself follows normal perfumery, so any fragrance benefit comes from the base scent; the added-compound effect on attraction has not been demonstrated in peer-reviewed studies.

paras: Wikipedia describes candidate human compounds including androstenol (1978 photo-rating study), androstenone (1983 skin-conductance changes reported by Van Toller and colleagues) and androstadienone, linked in some experiments to mood and attention to emotional faces [4]. Martha McClintock's 1971 report of menstrual synchrony was later questioned by reviewers, including Strassmann in 1999 and Yang and Schank in 2006 [4]. A 2019 study by Oren and colleagues reported that a putative pheromone affected men's sexual cognition [4].

The human vomeronasal organ, the structure many animals use to detect pheromones, appears atrophied or absent in adults and its receptor genes are nonfunctional, so whether humans detect pheromones through it is disputed [4]. Studying the subject is complicated because participants must be clean and odourless [4].

Grokipedia lists androstadienone for men's products, androstenone, androstenol and estratetraenol as typical ingredients, used at low concentrations in conventional fragrance bases [2]. It names RawChemistry For Him as a top-selling pheromone cologne on Amazon in early 2026 and Bad Wolf and A314 as niche options popular with enthusiasts [2].

Wikipedia reports some body-spray advertisers claim their products contain human sexual pheromones that act as aphrodisiacs [4]. Civetone, a musky compound sourced from civet oil and used as a perfume fixative, is sometimes called a pheromone for animals, and field biologists have used a cologne containing it to attract jaguars to camera traps [5].

Older T Nation threads from 2001 to 2003 ask whether pheromone colognes work; one poster using a pheromone-labelled cologne said it was hard to tell whether it worked and that women did not 'drop at my feet' [6], and another asked about androstenone-based products and their results [7]. A 2002 thread discusses an ingredient list resembling androstenone, androsterone and androstenol [8]. Other posters joke that their natural pheromones are enough [9]. A 2024 psychology-thread poster recalled an old study in which men told they wore an aphrodisiac cologne reported better success with women, which they framed as a confidence effect [10].

No studies found testing commercial pheromone colognes for attractiveness outcomes. Laboratory studies of individual compounds such as androstadienone and androstenol have examined mood, attention and photo ratings in small groups, with variable results [4].

timeline.event: Karlson and Luscher coin the term pheromone. [4]
McClintock reports menstrual synchrony; later questioned. [4]
Kirk-Smith study tests androstenol on photo ratings. [4]
Study by Oren and colleagues reports a putative pheromone affected men's sexual cognition. [4]

lore.intro: On T Nation, pheromone cologne is discussed from the early 2000s on, usually with curiosity about whether it works and often with jokes about natural musk [6][7][9].

claims.claim: Pheromone cologne makes women more attracted
claims.believers: Some posters tried pheromone products such as Realm and androstenone and asked whether they noticed an effect [6][7]. Marketing promises increased attractiveness [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behaviour (a disputed statement) and notes the field's small samples and publication bias [4].

claims.claim: Any benefit may be confidence or placebo
claims.believers: A T Nation poster recalled that men told they wore an aphrodisiac cologne reported more success with women [10].
claims.experts: Grokipedia states that perceived benefits are widely attributed to placebo or to the fragrance itself [2]. The study the poster recalls is not identified.

claims.claim: Natural body scent works as a pheromone signal
claims.believers: Posters joke that natural musk or pheromones are enough to attract partners [9].
claims.experts: Research on human sweat compounds has produced small mood and attention effects in lab settings [4].
